analysis.one_liner: Lets people delete their personal data from all data brokers with one FTC-run request.
analysis.headline: Introduced in April 2025 by a Republican senator with three Democratic cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and has had no hearing, markup, or vote since.
analysis.plain_summary: The DELETE Act would require companies that buy and sell people's personal information without a direct relationship to them to register with the Federal Trade Commission and publicly describe what they collect. It would then build a free government website where a person could submit one request to have every registered data broker delete their information and stop collecting it in the future. Brokers would have to check the system's secure registries at least every 31 days and delete matching records, subject to FTC enforcement and periodic independent audits.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people, especially those dealing with people-search sites, location-data brokers, and identity-theft or stalking risks. Today, removing your data requires finding dozens of brokers and filing separate opt-outs with each; this bill replaces that with one free request that covers all of them, and cuts off future collection unless you opt back in.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Anyone whose personal data data brokers sell

how_it_helps.text: A single submission through an FTC website would trigger deletion of the person's information at every registered data broker and its affiliates, and stop future collection unless the person says otherwise [S2].

The request would be free to the individual, and brokers would be required to check the FTC's secure registries at least every 31 days and delete any matching personal information within 31 days [S2].

Data brokers would have to register annually with the FTC, and their disclosures about what they collect and how people can opt out would be published in a downloadable, machine-readable format so the public can see who is trading their data [S2].

The FTC would enforce the rules the same way it enforces laws against unfair and deceptive practices, and each broker would undergo an independent third-party audit every three years to verify compliance [S2].
State privacy laws offering greater protection would remain in force, since the bill preempts state law only where it conflicts [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Data brokers and the marketing-data economy that buys from them. They would lose the personal information of anyone who opts out — permanently, covering future collection — and would bear registration, compliance, audit, and annual fee costs, with fees funding the FTC system.

drawbacks.text: The centralized system would hold salted, hashed copies of the email addresses, phone numbers, and home addresses of everyone who requests deletion. Hashing and separate salts per registry are required as safeguards, but a breach of that database would be a serious target for attackers, because it would be a verified list of real people's identifiers [S2].

The bill carves out several large categories of data handling: consumer reporting agencies, fraud prevention and identity verification, directory assistance, news gathering, and one-time asset-sale transfers are excluded from the definition of data broker, so a significant share of data collection would continue outside the deletion system [S2].

The FTC's public registry would carry a disclaimer that it cannot confirm the accuracy of what brokers report, and brokers would not have to disclose information claimed as a trade secret, limiting how much people can actually verify [S2].
Enforcement would rest solely with the FTC; individuals would have no right to sue a broker directly for failing to delete their data [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and large for individuals: one free, enforceable deletion request instead of chasing dozens of brokers, with future collection turned off by default. The design risks are manageable but real — the FTC database becomes a sensitive target, the industry carve-outs leave big chunks of data collection untouched, and the public registry is only as accurate as what brokers disclose. On balance, the bill would shift power over personal data from brokers back to the people the data describes.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee on the day it was introduced in April 2025, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote has been scheduled since.

narrative.text: Sen. Bill Cassidy introduced the bill on April 3, 2025, for himself and Democratic Sens. Ossoff and Luján [S2].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day [S4].
The cosponsor list shows three Democratic senators and no Republican cosponsors beyond the sponsor, and there have been no further committee or floor actions [S3].
Congress remains in session, so the bill is still alive but sits in committee with no scheduled action [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers keep selling and trading personal information under the current system, and people still have to opt out with each broker one by one.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data brokers; opt-outs remain one by one

sides.party_line_note: The bill has a Republican lead sponsor and its cosponsor list shows three Democratic senators; no committee action or vote has yet produced a party split.

industries.industry: Data brokers (people-search sites, location-data sellers, marketing data firms)
industries.note: These firms profit by compiling and selling information about people who have no relationship with them. The bill would force them to delete the records of anyone who files one request, permanently stop collecting that data, register publicly, submit to audits, and pay fees — cutting into their core business of reselling personal information. Because their revenue depends on using data that people cannot currently stop them from selling, their interest runs against the people the bill protects.

industries.industry: Digital advertising and marketing analytics firms that buy third-party data
industries.note: Their targeting and profiling depend on data flows from brokers. Every deletion request permanently removes a person from that supply, and opt-outs would compound over time, shrinking the audience data available for ad targeting.

industries.industry: Consumer reporting agencies and fraud-prevention services
industries.note: The bill explicitly excludes credit-reporting agencies, identity verification, and fraud prevention from its data broker definition, leaving their data practices outside the deletion system while competitors face it. For people, the carve-out preserves fraud checks and credit reports, but it also leaves a major segment of data collection untouched by the one-stop deletion right.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to the Senate Commerce Committee often go nowhere without a scheduled hearing, and this one has seen no action since its April 2025 introduction. With a Republican sponsor and small Democratic cosponsor list, its path forward would likely require committee consideration and floor time from party leadership; absent that, the most likely outcome is that it stays in committee for the rest of this Congress, as many privacy bills do.
